title: Shoftim: even the king reads (Deuteronomy 17:18–20)
hook: the king writes his own copy of the Torah so his heart isn't lifted up
tomorrow: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedek tzedek tirdof: pursue justice, and pursue it justly. Your line was justice, justice. Today, the law for the most powerful person in the land.

In the ancient world, a king was the law. His word settled things. His image was on the coins. Scribes carved his victories into stone. The idea that a king might have to sit down with a pen and copy out somebody else's law, by hand, every word, and then read it every day of his life, would have sounded absurd in most royal courts. Deuteronomy's chapter on kings is short, and mostly a list of limits. And it ends with an assignment.
screen: `THE KING WAS THE LAW.` → `COPY SOMEONE ELSE'S LAW?` → `A CHAPTER OF LIMITS.`

segments.voice: First the limits. If Israel sets a king over itself, he must not pile up horses, or take many wives, or heap up silver and gold. Power, pleasure, money: the three things kings usually collect. Then the assignment. In the old Jewish translation: when he sits on his throne, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book." And it shall be with him, "and he shall read therein all the days of his life." Why? The verse says it plainly: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren." The king is still one of them. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, adds that the king writes a scroll of his own, kept with him wherever he goes, even into battle. And it notes that every Jew is commanded to write a Torah scroll; the king just has an extra one. The phrase for a copy of this law is mishneh hatorah. It's where Deuteronomy gets its Greek name, second law. Over a thousand years later, Maimonides borrowed the same words for his great law code, the Mishneh Torah. The king reading every day is a picture of power under something bigger than itself: not the king's word over the law, but the law over the king's word. Reading isn't a reward for the powerful. It's a brake.
screen: `NOT HORSES, WIVES, OR GOLD.` · `WRITE HIM A COPY OF THIS LAW.` · `NOT LIFTED ABOVE HIS BROTHERS.` · `MISHNEH TORAH: SECOND LAW.` · then, large: `EVEN THE KING READS.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you hold some power: a parent, a manager, the one who knows most in the room, the oldest sibling. Bring to mind a line, from scripture, a teacher or your grandmother, that puts that power back in its place, something like: you are one of them. Say it slowly, twice, and let it sit above you for a minute.
Shoftim. Judges. The portion where even the king must write the law down and read it every day.
Your line: even the king reads. A week of tzedakah, the release, simcha, giving by your blessing, judges at the gates, and justice twice. That's day five hundred four.

howItsDone: Jewish law counts writing a Torah scroll as a commandment for every Jew; many fulfill it today by sponsoring or writing a single letter in a community's new scroll, and the king's special scroll is discussed in the Talmud and Maimonides.

chat.says: Why would the Torah make a king copy out the law and read it every day?
options: So his heart isn't lifted above his brothers; the law stands over the king, and reading is a brake.
So he can memorize it and become the final judge of what the law means for everyone else.
So everyone sees his learning; copying the law proves the king is wiser than his people.
chat.meaning: Deuteronomy says the king writes and reads the law all his life so that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren.

Shoftim.meaning: judges; the portion that limits even the king
